Most people say it is worth it, and most of them are not paying for a family.

The offer looked enormous. I remember converting it in my head on the train home and thinking that we would be considerably better off than in Sao Paulo. What I had not converted was anything else. Tax and national insurance took a much larger bite than I expected, so the take-home pay was already a good deal smaller than the number I had been celebrating. Then the deposit: six weeks of rent, held, plus the first month, in the same fortnight as two flights and a shipping container. For the first three months we scraped by on a salary that in Portuguese sounds like a lot of money. It got better, and I would do it again, but I would tell anybody moving to work out the disposable income first and ignore the headline entirely. The headline is the one number that never touches your life.

I have placed people in this city for eleven years, and the conversation that decides whether somebody stays is never about salary. It is about the trade-off between space and time. People move further out because the flats are far bigger and the rent is a little lower, and they underestimate the commute every single time. Twenty minutes further out is nothing, and it buys you slightly more room. Forty minutes further out is a different life: it is nearly seven hours a week, which is far more than anybody budgets for, and it is the hours at both ends of the day, which are the ones that matter. My advice is unfashionable. Take the smaller flat closer in for the first year, find out where your life actually happens, and move once you know. Moving twice is expensive. Commuting for two years is much more expensive, and you pay for it in something you cannot get back.

The offer arrives and the number looks considerably better than the current salary. Tax takes a much larger bite than expected, so the take-home pay is smaller than the headline. The deposit and the first month of rent have to be found in the same fortnight as the flights. The flat further out is chosen, because it is far bigger and slightly cheaper. And the commute turns out to cost nearly seven hours a week, which nobody had budgeted for.
